entries.62243d8f1c45db778016a3e1566ba53926122e76: <div sID="gen9560" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Job.14" sID="Job.14"/> <div eID="gen9560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9561" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9562" type="x-p"/> Job had turned from speaking to his friends, finding it to no purpose to reason with them, and here he goes on to speak to God and himself. He had reminded his friends of their frailty and mortality (<reference osisRef="Job.13.12">ch. xiii. 12</reference>); here he reminds himself of his own, and pleads it with God for some mitigation of his miseries. We have here an account, I. Of man's life, that it is, 1. Short, <reference osisRef="Job.14.1">ver. 1</reference>. 2. Sorrowful, <reference osisRef="Job.14.1">ver. 1</reference>. 3. Sinful, <reference osisRef="Job.14.4">ver. 4</reference>. 4. Stinted, <reference osisRef="Job.14.5">ver. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.14.14">14</reference>. II. Of man's death, that it puts a final period to our present life, to which we shall not again return (<reference osisRef="Job.14.7-Job.14.12">ver. 7-12</reference>), that it hides us from the calamities of life (<reference osisRef="Job.14.13">ver. 13</reference>), destroys the hopes of life (<reference osisRef="Job.14.18-Job.14.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>), sends us away from the business of life (<reference osisRef="Job.14.20">ver. 20</reference>), and keeps us in the dark concerning our relations in this life, how much soever we have formerly been in care about them <reference osisRef="Job.14.21-Job.14.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. III. The use Job makes of all this. 1. He pleads it with God, who, he thought, was too strict and severe with him (<reference osisRef="Job.14.16-Job.14.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>), begging that, in consideration of his frailty, he would not contend with him (<reference osisRef="Job.14.3">ver. 3</reference>), but grant him some respite, <reference osisRef="Job.14.6">ver. 6</reference>. 2. He engages himself to prepare for death (<reference osisRef="Job.14.14">ver. 14</reference>), and encourages himself to hope that it would be comfortable to him, <reference osisRef="Job.14.15">ver. 15</reference>. This chapter is proper for funeral solemnities; and serious meditations on it will help us both to get good by the death of others and to get ready for our own.
entries.4b0f0f70b74ea64b6d580e2688efda5a63c1c559: <div eID="gen9562" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9561" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Brevity and Frailty of Human Life. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9563" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Man <hi type="italic">that is</hi> born of a woman <hi type="italic">is</hi> of few days, and full of trouble. <hi type="super">2</hi> He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not. <hi type="super">3</hi> And dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one, and bringest me into judgment with thee? <hi type="super">4</hi> Who can bring a clean <hi type="italic">thing</hi> out of an unclean? not one. <hi type="super">5</hi> Seeing his days <hi type="italic">are</hi> determined, the number of his months <hi type="italic">are</hi> with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass; <hi type="super">6</hi> Turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as a hireling, his day. <div eID="gen9563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9564" type="x-p"/> We are here led to think, <div eID="gen9564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9565" type="x-p"/> I. Of the original of human life. God is indeed its great original, for he <hi type="italic">breathed into man the breath of life</hi> and in him we live; but we date it from our birth, and thence we must date both its frailty and its pollution. 1. Its frailty: <hi type="italic">Man, that is born of a woman, is</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">of few days,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.1">v. 1</reference>. This may refer to the first woman, who was called <hi type="italic">Eve,</hi> because she was the mother of all living. Of her, who being deceived by the tempter was first in the transgression, we are all born, and consequently derive from her that sin and corruption which both shorten our days and sadden them. Or it may refer to every man's immediate mother. The woman is the weaker vessel, and we know that <hi type="italic">partus sequitur ventrem—the child takes after the mother.</hi> Let not the strong man therefore glory in his strength, or in the strength of his father, but remember that he is born of a woman, and that, when God pleases, the <hi type="italic">mighty men become as women,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.30">Jer. li. 30</reference>. 2. Its pollution (<reference osisRef="Job.14.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?</hi> If man be born of a woman that is a sinner, how can it be otherwise than that he should be a sinner? See <reference osisRef="Job.25.4">ch. xxv. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">How can he be clean that is born of a woman?</hi> Clean children cannot come from unclean parents any more than pure streams from an impure spring or grapes from thorns. Our habitual corruption is derived with our nature from our parents, and is therefore bred in the bone. Our blood is not only attainted by a legal conviction, but tainted with an hereditary disease. Our Lord Jesus, being made sin for us, is said to be <hi type="italic">made of a woman,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Gal. iv. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen9565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9566" type="x-p"/> II. Of the nature of human life: it is <hi type="italic">a flower,</hi> it is a <hi type="italic">shadow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">v. 2</reference>. The flower is fading, and all its beauty soon withers and is gone. The shadow is fleeting, and its very being will soon be lost and drowned in the shadows of the night. Of neither do we make any account; in neither do we put any confidence. <div eID="gen9566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9567" type="x-p"/> III. Of the shortness and uncertainty of human life: Man is <hi type="italic">of few days.</hi> Life is here computed, not by months or years, but by days, for we cannot be sure of any day but that it may be our last. These days are few, fewer than we think of, few at the most, in comparison with the days of the first patriarchs, much more in comparison with the days of eternity, but much fewer to most, who come short of what we call <hi type="italic">the age of man.</hi> Man sometimes no sooner comes forth than he <hi type="italic">is cut down</hi>—comes forth out of the womb than he dies in the cradle—comes forth into the world and enters into the business of it than he is hurried away as soon as he has laid his hand to the plough. If not cut down immediately, yet <hi type="italic">he flees as a shadow,</hi> and never continues in one stay, in one shape, but the fashion of it passes away; so does this world, and our life in it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.31">1 Cor. vii. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen9567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9568" type="x-p"/> IV. Of the calamitous state of human life. Man, as he is short-lived, so he is sad-lived. Though he had but a few days to spend here, yet, if he might rejoice in those few, it were well (a short life and a merry one is the boast of some); but it is not so. During these few days he is <hi type="italic">full of trouble,</hi> not only troubled, but full of trouble, either toiling or fretting, grieving or fearing. No day passes without some vexation, some hurry, some disorder or other. Those that are fond of the world shall have enough of it. He is <hi type="italic">satur tremore—full of commotion.</hi> The fewness of his days creates him a continual trouble and uneasiness in expectation of the period of them, and he always hangs in doubt of his life. Yet, since man's days are so full of trouble, it is well that they are few, that the soul's imprisonment in the body, and banishment from the Lord, are not perpetual, are not long. When we come to heaven our days will be many, and perfectly free from trouble, and in the mean time faith, hope, and love, balance the present grievances. <div eID="gen9568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9569" type="x-p"/> V. Of the sinfulness of human life, arising from the sinfulness of the human nature. So some understand that question (<reference osisRef="Job.14.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?</hi>—a clean performance from an unclean principle? Note, Actual transgressions are the natural product of habitual corruption, which is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> called <hi type="italic">original</hi> sin, because it is the original of all our sins. This holy Job here laments, as all that are sanctified do, running up the streams to the fountain (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.5">Ps. li. 5</reference>); and some think he intends it as a plea with God for compassion: "Lord, be not extreme to mark my sins of human frailty and infirmity, for thou knowest my weakness. <hi type="italic">O remember that I am flesh!</hi>" The Chaldee paraphrase has an observable reading of this verse: <hi type="italic">Who can make a man clean that is polluted with sin? Cannot one? that is, God. Or who but God, who is one, and will spare him?</hi> God, by his almighty grace, can change the skin of the Ethiopian, the skin of Job, though clothed with worms. <div eID="gen9569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9570" type="x-p"/> VI. Of the settled period of human life, <reference osisRef="Job.14.5">v. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen9570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9571" type="x-p"/> 1. Three things we are here assured of:— (1.) That our life will come to an end; our days upon earth are not numberless, are not endless, no, they are numbered, and will soon be finished, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.26">Dan. v. 26</reference>. (2.) That it is determined, in the counsel and decree of God, how long we shall live and when we shall die. The number of our months is with God, at the disposal of his power, which cannot be controlled, and under the view of his omniscience, which cannot be deceived. It is certain that God's providence has the ordering of the period of our lives; our times are in his hand. The powers of nature depend upon him, and act under him. In him we live and move. Diseases are his servants; he kills and makes alive. Nothing comes to pass by chance, no, not the execution done by a bow drawn at a venture. It is therefore certain that God's prescience has determined it before; for <hi type="italic">known unto God are all his works.</hi> Whatever he does he determined, yet with a regard partly to the settled course of nature (the end and the means are determined together) and to the settled rules of moral government, punishing evil and rewarding good in this life. We are no more governed by the Stoic's blind fate than by the Epicurean's blind fortune. (3.) That the bounds God has fixed we cannot pass; for his counsels are unalterable, his foresight being infallible. <div eID="gen9571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9572" type="x-p"/> 2. These considerations Job here urges as reasons, (1.) Why God should not be so strict in taking cognizance of him and of his slips and failings (<reference osisRef="Job.14.3">v. 3</reference>): "Since I have such a corrupt nature within, and am liable to so much trouble, which is a constant temptation from without, <hi type="italic">dost thou open thy eyes</hi> and fasten them <hi type="italic">upon such a one,</hi> extremely to mark what I do amiss? <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">ch. xiii. 27</reference>. And dost thou <hi type="italic">bring me,</hi> such a worthless worm as I am, <hi type="italic">into judgment with thee</hi> who art so quick sighted to discover the least failing, so holy to hate it, so just to condemn it, and so mighty to punish it?" The consideration of our own inability to contend with God, of our own sinfulness and weakness, should engage us to pray, <hi type="italic">Lord, enter not into judgment with thy servant.</hi> (2.) Why he should not be so severe in his dealings with him: "Lord, I have but a little time to live. I must certainly and shortly go hence, and the few days I have to spend here are, at the best, full of trouble. O let me have a little respite! <reference osisRef="Job.14.6">v. 6</reference>. Turn from afflicting a poor creature thus, and let him rest awhile; allow him some breathing time, <hi type="italic">until he shall accomplish as a hireling his day.</hi> It is appointed to me once to die; let that one day suffice me, and let me not thus be continually dying, dying a thousand deaths. Let it suffice that my life, at best, is <hi type="italic">as the day of a hireling,</hi> a day of toil and labour. I am content to accomplish that, and will make the best of the common hardships of human life, the burden and heat of the day; but let me not feel those uncommon tortures, let not my life be as the day of a malefactor, all execution-day." Thus may we find some relief under great troubles by recommending ourselves to the compassion of that God who knows our frame and will consider it, and our being out of frame too.
entries.c71d57285ddf597e9c46e3867aeb847c3c37be50: <div eID="gen9572" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Death Anticipated. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9573" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. <hi type="super">8</hi> Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">Yet</hi> through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. <hi type="super">10</hi> But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where <hi type="italic">is</hi> he? <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> the waters fail from the sea, and the flood decayeth and drieth up: 12 So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens <hi type="italic">be</hi> no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep. <hi type="super">13</hi> O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me! <hi type="super">14</hi> If a man die, shall he live <hi type="italic">again?</hi> all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands. <div eID="gen9573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9574" type="x-p"/> We have seen what Job has to say concerning life; let us now see what he has to say concerning death, which his thoughts were very much conversant with, now that he was sick and sore. It is not unseasonable, when we are in health, to think of dying; but it is an inexcusable incogitancy if, when we are already taken into the custody of death's messengers, we look upon it as a thing at a distance. Job had already shown that death will come, and that its hour is already fixed. Now here he shows, <div eID="gen9574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9575" type="x-p"/> I. That death is a removal for ever out of this world. This he had spoken of before (<reference osisRef="Job.7.9-Job.7.10">ch. vii. 9, 10</reference>), and now he mentions it again; for, though it be a truth that needs not be proved, yet it needs to be much considered, that it may be duly improved. <div eID="gen9575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9576" type="x-p"/> 1. A man cut down by death will not revive again, as a tree cut down will. What hope there is of a tree he shows very elegantly, <reference osisRef="Job.14.7-Job.14.9">v. 7-9</reference>. If the body of the tree be cut down, and only the stem or stump left in the ground, though it seem dead and dry, yet it will shoot out young boughs again, as if it were but newly planted. The moisture of the earth and the rain of heaven are, as it were, scented and perceived by the stump of a tree, and they have an influence upon it to revive it; but the dead body of a man would not perceive them, nor be in the least affected by them. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream, when his being deprived of the use of his reason was signified by the cutting down of a tree, his return to it again was signified by the leaving of the stump in the earth with a band of iron and brass to be <hi type="italic">wet with the dew of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.15">Dan. iv. 15</reference>. But man has no such prospect of a return to life. The vegetable life is a cheap and easy thing: the scent of water will recover it. The animal life, in some insects and fowls, is so: the heat of the sun retrieves it. But the rational soul, when once retired, is too great, too noble, a thing to be recalled by any of the powers of nature; it is out of the reach of sun or rain, and cannot be restored but by the immediate operations of Omnipotence itself; for (<reference osisRef="Job.14.10">v. 10</reference>) <hi type="italic">man dieth and wasteth, away, yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?</hi> Two words are here used for man:—<hi type="italic">Geber, a mighty man,</hi> though mighty, dies; <hi type="italic">Adam, a man of the earth,</hi> because earthy, gives up the ghost. Note, Man is a dying creature. He is here described by what occurs, (1.) Before death: he <hi type="italic">wastes away;</hi> he is continually wasting, dying daily, spending upon the quick stock of life. Sickness and old age are wasting things to the flesh, the strength, the beauty. (2.) In death: <hi type="italic">he gives up the ghost;</hi> the soul leaves the body, and returns to God who gave it, the Father of spirits. (3.) After death: <hi type="italic">Where is he?</hi> He is not where he was; his place knows him no more; but <hi type="italic">is he nowhere?</hi> So some read it. Yes, he is somewhere; and it is a very awful consideration to think where those are that have given up the ghost, and where we shall be when we give it up. It has gone to the world of spirits, gone into eternity, gone to return no more to this world. <div eID="gen9576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9577" type="x-p"/> 2. A man laid down in the grave will not rise up again, <reference osisRef="Job.14.11-Job.14.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Every night we lie down to sleep, and in the morning we awake and rise again; but at death we must lie down in the grave, not to awake or rise again to such a world, such a state, as we are now in, never to awake or arise <hi type="italic">until the heavens,</hi> the faithful measures of time, shall <hi type="italic">be no more,</hi> and consequently time itself shall come to an end and be swallowed up in eternity; so that the life of man may fitly be compared to the waters of a land-flood, which spread far and make a great show, but they are shallow, and when they are cut off from the sea or river, the swelling and overflowing of which was the cause of them, they soon decay and dry up, and their place knows them no more. The waters of life are soon exhaled and disappear. The body, like some of those waters, sinks and soaks into the earth, and is buried there; the soul, like others of them, is drawn upwards, to mingle with the waters above the firmament. The learned Sir Richard Blackmore makes this also to be a dissimilitude. If the waters decay and be dried up in the summer, yet they will return again in the winter; but it is not so with the life of man. Take part of his paraphrase in his own words:— <div eID="gen9577" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen9578"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9579"/>A flowing river, or a standing lake,<l eID="gen9579" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9580"/>May their dry banks and naked shores forsake;<l eID="gen9580" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9581"/>Their waters may exhale and upward move,<l eID="gen9581" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9582"/>Their channel leave to roll in clouds above;<l eID="gen9582" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9583"/>But the returning water will restore<l eID="gen9583" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9584"/>What in the summer they had lost before:<l eID="gen9584" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9585"/>But if, O man! thy vital streams desert<l eID="gen9585" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9586"/>Their purple channels and defraud the heart,<l eID="gen9586" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9587"/>With fresh recruits they ne'er will be supplied,<l eID="gen9587" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9588"/>Nor feel their leaping life's returning tide.<l eID="gen9588" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen9578"/> <div sID="gen9589" type="x-p"/> II. That yet there will be a return of man to life again in another world, at the end of time, when <hi type="italic">the heavens</hi> are <hi type="italic">no more.</hi> Then <hi type="italic">they shall awake and be raised out of their sleep.</hi> The resurrection of the dead was doubtless an article of Job's creed, as appears, <reference osisRef="Job.19.26">ch. xix. 26</reference>, and to that, it should seem, he has an eye here, where, in the belief of that, we have three things:— <div eID="gen9589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9590" type="x-p"/> 1. A humble petition for a hiding-place in the grave, <reference osisRef="Job.14.13">v. 13</reference>. It was not only a passionate weariness of this life that he wished to die, but in a pious assurance of a better life, to which at length he should arise. <hi type="italic">O that thou wouldst hide me in the grave!</hi> The grave is not only a resting-place, but a hiding-place, to the people of God. God has the key of the grave, to let in now and to let out at the resurrection. He <hi type="italic">hides men in the grave,</hi> as we hide our treasure in a place of secresy and safety; and he who hides will find, and nothing shall be lost. "O that thou wouldst hide me, not only from the storms and troubles of this life, but for the bliss and glory of a better life! Let me lie in the grave, reserved for immortality, in secret from all the world, but not from thee, not from those eyes which saw my substance when first curiously wrought in <hi type="italic">the lowest parts of the earth,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15-Ps.139.16">Ps. cxxxix. 15, 16</reference>. There let me lie, (1.) <hi type="italic">Until thy wrath be past.</hi> As long as the bodies of the saints lie in the grave, so long there are some remains of that wrath which they were by nature children of, so long they are under some of the effects of sin; but, when the body is raised, it is wholly past—death, the last enemy, will then be totally destroyed. (2.) Until the <hi type="italic">set time</hi> comes for my being remembered, as Noah was remembered in the ark (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.1">Gen. viii. 1</reference>), where God not only hid him from the destruction of the old world, but reserved him for the reparation of a new world. The bodies of the saints shall not be forgotten in the grave. There is a time appointed, a time set, for their being enquired after. We cannot be sure that we shall look through the darkness of our present troubles and see good days after them in this world; but, if we can but get well to the grave, we may with an eye of faith look through the darkness of that, as Job here, and see better days on the other side of it, in a better world. <div eID="gen9590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9591" type="x-p"/> 2. A holy resolution patiently to attend the will of God both in his death and his resurrection (<reference osisRef="Job.14.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">If a man die, shall he live again? All the days of my appointed time will I wait until my change come.</hi> Job's friends proving miserable comforters, he set himself to be the more his own comforter. His case was now bad, but he pleases himself with the expectation of a change. I think it cannot be meant of his return to a prosperous condition in this world. His friends indeed flattered him with the hopes of that, but he himself all along despaired of it. Comforts founded upon uncertainties at best must needs be uncertain comforts; and therefore, no doubt, it is something more sure than that which he here bears up himself with the expectation of. The change he waits for must therefore be understood either, (1.) Of the change of the resurrection, when the vile body shall be changed (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Phil. iii. 21</reference>), and a great and glorious change it will be; and then that question, <hi type="italic">If a man die, shall he live again?</hi> must be taken by way of admiration. "Strange! Shall these dry bones live! If so, all the time appointed for the continuance of the separation between soul and body my separate soul shall wait until that change comes, when it shall be united again to the body, <hi type="italic">and my flesh also shall rest in hope.</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.16.9">Ps. xvi. 9</reference>. Or, (2.) Of the change at death. "<hi type="italic">If a man die, shall he live again?</hi> No, not such a life as he now lives; and therefore I will patiently wait until that change comes which will put a period to my calamities, and not impatiently wish for the anticipation of it, as I have done." Observe here, [1.] That it is a serious thing to die; it is a work by itself. It is a change; there is a visible change in the body, its appearance altered, its actions brought to an end, but a greater change with the soul, which quits the body, and removes to the world of spirits, finishes its state of probation and enters upon that of retribution. This change will come, and it will be a final change, not like the transmutations of the elements, which return to their former state. No, we must die, not thus to live again. It is but once to die, and that had need be well done that is to be done but once. An error here is fatal, conclusive, and not again to be rectified. [2.] That therefore it is the duty of every one of us to wait for that change, and to continue waiting all the days of our appointed time. The time of life is an appointed time; that time is to be reckoned by days; and those days are to be spent in waiting for our change. That is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We must expect that it will come, and think much of it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We must desire that it would come, as those that long to be with Christ. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> We must be willing to tarry until it does come, as those that believe God's time to be the best. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> We must give diligence to get ready against it comes, that it may be a blessed change to us. <div eID="gen9591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9592" type="x-p"/> 3. A joyful expectation of bliss and satisfaction in this (<reference osisRef="Job.14.15">v. 15</reference>): Then <hi type="italic">thou shalt call, and I will answer thee.</hi> Now, he was under such a cloud that he could not, he durst not, answer (<reference osisRef="Job.9.15 Job.9.35">ch. ix. 15, 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.22">xiii. 22</reference>); but he comforted himself with this, that there would come a time when God would call and he should answer. Then, that is, (1.) At the resurrection, "Thou shalt call me out of the grave, by the voice of the archangel, and I will answer and come at the call." The body is the <hi type="italic">work of God's hands,</hi> and he will have a desire to that, having prepared a glory for it. Or, (2.) At death: "Thou shalt call my body to the grave, and my soul to thyself, and I will answer, Ready, Lord, ready—Coming, coming; here I am." Gracious souls can cheerfully answer death's summons, and appear to his writ. Their spirits are not forcibly required from them (as <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 20</reference>), but willingly resigned by them, and the earthly tabernacle not violently pulled down, but voluntarily laid down, with this assurance, "Thou <hi type="italic">wilt have a desire to the work of thy hands.</hi> Thou hast mercy in store for me, not only as made by thy providence, but new-made by thy grace;" otherwise <hi type="italic">he that made them will not save them.</hi> Note, Grace in the soul is the work of God's own hands, and therefore he will not forsake it in this world (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">Ps. cxxxviii. 8</reference>), but will have a desire to it, to perfect it in the other, and to crown it with endless glory.
entries.fc28cf12de606b4d35a3d5d41e7b4724e98fbede: <div eID="gen9592" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Complainings of Job. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9593" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> For now thou numberest my steps: dost thou not watch over my sin? <hi type="super">17</hi> My transgression <hi type="italic">is</hi> sealed up in a bag, and thou sewest up mine iniquity. <hi type="super">18</hi> And surely the mountain falling cometh to nought, and the rock is removed out of his place. <hi type="super">19</hi> The waters wear the stones: thou washest away the things which grow <hi type="italic">out</hi> of the dust of the earth; and thou destroyest the hope of man. <hi type="super">20</hi> Thou prevailest for ever against him, and he passeth: thou changest his countenance, and sendest him away. <hi type="super">21</hi> His sons come to honour, and he knoweth <hi type="italic">it</hi> not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth <hi type="italic">it</hi> not of them. <hi type="super">22</hi> But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn. <div eID="gen9593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9594" type="x-p"/> Job here returns to his complaints; and, though he is not without hope of future bliss, he finds it very hard to get over his present grievances. <div eID="gen9594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9595" type="x-p"/> I. He complains of the particular hardships he apprehended himself under from the strictness of God's justice, <reference osisRef="Job.14.16-Job.14.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he longed to go hence to that world where God's wrath will be past, because now he was under the continual tokens of it, as a child, under the severe discipline of the rod, longs to be of age. "When shall my change come? <hi type="italic">For now thou</hi> seemest to me to <hi type="italic">number my steps,</hi> and <hi type="italic">watch over my sin,</hi> and <hi type="italic">seal it up in a bag,</hi> as bills of indictment are kept safely, to be produced against the prisoner." See <reference osisRef="Deut.32.34">Deut. xxxii. 34</reference>. "Thou takest all advantages against me; old scores are called over, every infirmity is animadverted upon, and no sooner is a false step taken than I am beaten for it." Now, 1. Job does right to the divine justice in owning that he smarted for his sins and transgressions, that he had done enough to deserve all that was laid upon him; for there was sin in all his steps, and he was guilty of transgression enough to bring all this ruin upon him, if it were strictly enquired into: he is far from saying that he perishes being innocent. But, 2. He does wrong to the divine goodness in suggesting that God was extreme to mark what he did amiss, and made the worst of every thing. He spoke to this purport, <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">ch. xiii. 27</reference>. It was unadvisedly said, and therefore we will not dwell too much upon it. God does indeed see all our sins; he sees sin in his own people; but he is not severe in reckoning with us, nor is the law ever stretched against us, but we are punished less than our iniquities deserve. God does indeed seal and sew up, against the day of wrath, the transgression of the impenitent, but the sins of his people he blots out as a cloud. <div eID="gen9595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9596" type="x-p"/> II. He complains of the wasting condition of mankind in general. We live in a dying world. <hi type="italic">Who knows the power of God's anger, by which we are consumed and troubled, and in which all our days are passed away?</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.90.7-Ps.90.9">Ps. xc. 7-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">11</reference>. And who can bear up against his rebukes? <reference osisRef="Ps.39.11">Ps. xxxix. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen9596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9597" type="x-p"/> 1. We see the decays of the earth itself. (1.) Of the strongest parts of it, <reference osisRef="Job.14.18">v. 18</reference>. Nothing will last always, for we see even mountains moulder and come to nought; they wither and fall as a leaf; rocks wax old and pass away by the continual beating of the sea against them. <hi type="italic">The waters wear the stones</hi> with constant dropping, <hi type="italic">non vi, sed sæpe cadendo—not by the violence, but by the constancy with which they fall.</hi> On this earth every thing is the worse for the wearing. <hi type="italic">Tempus edax rerum—Time devours all things.</hi> It is not so with the heavenly bodies. (2.) Of the natural products of it. The things which grow out of the earth, and seem to be firmly rooted in it, are sometimes by an excess of rain washed away, <reference osisRef="Job.14.19">v. 19</reference>. Some think he pleads this for relief: "Lord, my patience will not hold out always; even rocks and mountains will fail at last; therefore cease the controversy." <div eID="gen9597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9598" type="x-p"/> 2. No marvel then if we see the decays of man upon the earth, for he is of the earth, earthy. Job begins to think his case is not singular, and therefore he ought to reconcile himself to the common lot. We perceive by many instances, (1.) How vain it is to expect much from the enjoyments of life: "<hi type="italic">Thou destroyest the hope of man,</hi>" that is, "puttest an end to all the projects he had framed and all the prospects of satisfaction he had flattered himself with." Death will be the destruction of all those hopes which are built upon worldly confidences and confined to worldly comforts. Hope in Christ, and hope in heaven, death will consummate and not destroy. (2.) How vain it is to struggle against the assaults of death (<reference osisRef="Job.14.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou prevailest for ever against him.</hi> Note, Man is an unequal match for God. Whom God contends with he will certainly prevail against, prevail for ever against so that they shall never be able to make head again. Note further, The stroke of death is irresistible; it is to no purpose to dispute its summons. God prevails against man and he passes away, and lo he is not. Look upon a dying man, and see, [1.] How his looks are altered: <hi type="italic">Thou changest his countenance,</hi> and this in two ways:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> By the disease of his body. When a man has been a few days sick what a change is there in his countenance! How much more when he has been a few minutes dead! The countenance which was majestic and awful becomes mean and despicable—that was lovely and amiable becomes ghastly and frightful. <hi type="italic">Bury my dead out of my sight.</hi> Where then is the admired beauty? Death changes the countenance, and then sends us away out of this world, gives us one dismission hence, never to return. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By the discomposure of his mind. Note, The approach of death will make the strongest and stoutest to change countenance; it will make the most merry smiling countenance to look grave and serious, and the most bold daring countenance to look pale and timorous. [2.] How little he is concerned in the affairs of his family, which once lay so near his heart. When he is in the hands of the harbingers of death, suppose struck with a palsy or apoplexy, or delirious in a fever, or in conflict with death, tell him then the most agreeable news, or the most painful, concerning his children, it is all alike, he knows it not, he perceives it not, <reference osisRef="Job.14.21">v. 21</reference>. He is going to that world where he will be a perfect stranger to all those things which here filled and affected him. The consideration of this should moderate our cares concerning our children and families. God will know what comes of them when we are gone. To him therefore let us commit them, with him let us leave them, and not burden ourselves with needless fruitless cares concerning them. [3.] How dreadful the agonies of death are (<reference osisRef="Job.14.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">While his flesh is upon him</hi> (so it may be read), that is, the body he is so loth to lay down,: <hi type="italic">it shall have pain; and while his soul is within him,</hi> that is, the spirit he is so loth to resign, it shall mourn. Note, Dying work is hard work; dying pangs are, commonly, sore pangs. It is folly therefore for men to defer their repentance to a death-bed, and to have that to do which is the one thing needful when they are really unfit to do any thing: but it is true wisdom by making our peace with God in Christ and keeping a good conscience, to treasure up comforts which will support and relieve us against the pains and sorrows of a dying hour.  <chapter eID="Job.14"/> <div eID="gen9598" type="x-p"/>

entries.4090513fd9e00dc64fd0b28fa5573be17f2a43c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4736"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.14.1-Job.14.22">Job 14:1-22</reference>. Job Passes from His Own to the Common Misery of Mankind.</title> <div sID="gen6881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4736"/><hi type="bold">1. woman--</hi>feeble, and in the East looked down upon (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.21">Ge 2:21</reference>). Man being born of one so frail must be frail himself (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.11">Mt 11:11</reference>).<div eID="gen6881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">few days--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.47.9">Ge 47:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Psa 90:10</reference>). Literally, "short of days." Man is the reverse of full of days and short of trouble. <div eID="gen6882" type="x-p"/>
entries.60abc1e40df6cb643e0fd220afa97df9c36f05a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4737"/><div sID="gen6883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4737"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.6">Psa 90:6</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">Job 8:9</reference>). <div eID="gen6883" type="x-p"/>
entries.01575813c7b853e18c8fd963048442411de2c2a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4738"/><div sID="gen6884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4738"/><hi type="bold">3. open ... eyes upon--</hi>Not in graciousness; but, "Dost Thou sharply fix Thine eyes upon?" (See on <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>; also see on <reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job 1:7</reference>). Is one so frail as man worthy of such constant watching on the part of God? (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.4">Zec 12:4</reference>).<div eID="gen6884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">me--</hi>so frail.<div eID="gen6885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thee--</hi>so almighty. <div eID="gen6886" type="x-p"/>
entries.11dbd654554ef7e888fe033e9b6f9a4e5705e235: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4739"/><div sID="gen6887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4739"/>4. A plea in mitigation. The doctrine of original sin was held from the first. "Man is unclean from his birth, how then can God expect perfect cleanness from such a one and deal so severely with me?" <div eID="gen6887" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb237154d3571bed07f9eaaa4a38ca1f9833f0a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4740"/><div sID="gen6888" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4740"/><hi type="bold">5. determined--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.7.1">Job 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">Is 10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">11:36</reference>). <div eID="gen6888" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6670782ada3da413c2d0ba9dfc03fca210396d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4741"/><div sID="gen6889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4741"/><hi type="bold">6. Turn--</hi>namely, Thine eyes from watching him so jealously (<reference osisRef="Job.14.3">Job 14:3</reference>).<div eID="gen6889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hireling--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.7.1">Job 7:1</reference>).<div eID="gen6890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accomplish--</hi>rather, "enjoy." That he may at least enjoy the measure of rest of the hireling who though hard worked reconciles himself to his lot by the hope of his rest and reward [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6891" type="x-p"/>
entries.b00885fc232e7993269d6033045cd0e1df477486: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4742"/><div sID="gen6892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4742"/>7. Man may the more claim a peaceful life, since, when separated from it by death, he never returns to it. This does not deny a future life, but a return to the present condition of life. Job plainly hopes for a future state (<reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.7.2">Job 7:2</reference>). Still, it is but vague and trembling hope, not assurance; excepting the one bright glimpse in <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>. The Gospel revelation was needed to change fears, hopes, and glimpses into clear and definite certainties. <div eID="gen6892" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f82dc4c6be886caa3de81c9b2158d296f2ba9fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4743"/><div sID="gen6893" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4743"/><hi type="bold">9. scent--</hi>exhalation, which, rather than the humidity of water, causes the tree to germinate. In the antithesis to man the tree is personified, and volition is poetically ascribed to it.<div eID="gen6893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like a plant--</hi>"as if newly planted" [Umbreit]; not as if trees and plants were a different species. <div eID="gen6894" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f120c5ca51a4c6682112e0d7f99ea62e6280165: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4744"/><div sID="gen6895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4744"/><hi type="bold">10. man ... man--</hi>Two distinct Hebrew words are here used; Geber, a mighty man: though mighty, he dies. Adam, a man of earth: because earthly, he gives up the ghost.<div eID="gen6895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wasteth--</hi>is reduced to nothing: he cannot revive in the present state, as the tree does. The cypress and pine, which when cut down do not revive, were the symbols of death among the Romans. <div eID="gen6896" type="x-p"/>
entries.3851a8cb7072adb496084dd69dc949acc8168173: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4745"/><div sID="gen6897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4745"/><hi type="bold">11. sea--</hi>that is, a lake, or pool formed from the outspreading of a river. Job lived near the Euphrates: and "sea" is applied to it (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.36">Jr 51:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>). So of the Nile (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">Is 19:5</reference>).<div eID="gen6897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fail--</hi>utterly disappeared by drying up. The rugged channel of the once flowing water answers to the outstretched corpse ("lieth down," <reference osisRef="Job.14.12">Job 14:12</reference>) of the once living man. <div eID="gen6898" type="x-p"/>
entries.44d7108dea3b6c12128b41b650272de1e0015d9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4746"/><div sID="gen6899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4746"/><hi type="bold">12. heavens be no more--</hi>This only implies that Job had no hope of living again in the present order of the world, not that he had no hope of life again in a new order of things. <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Psa 102:26</reference> proves that early under the Old Testament the dissolution of the present earth and heavens was expected (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.8.22">Ge 8:22</reference>). Enoch before Job had implied that the "saints shall live again" (Jude 14; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.13-Heb.11.16">He 11:13-16</reference>). Even if, by this phrase, Job meant "never" (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">Psa 89:29</reference>) in his gloomier state of feelings, yet the Holy Ghost has made him unconsciously (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>) use language expressing the truth, that the resurrection is to be preceded by the dissolution of the heavens. In <reference osisRef="Job.14.13-Job.14.15">Job 14:13-15</reference> he plainly passes to brighter hopes of a world to come. <div eID="gen6899" type="x-p"/>
entries.9322645134b8c4667d7e6b50ebb03b90649ae446: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4747"/><div sID="gen6900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4747"/>13. Job wishes to be kept hidden in the grave until God's wrath against him shall have passed away. So while God's wrath is visiting the earth for the abounding apostasy which is to precede the second coming, God's people shall be hidden against the resurrection glory (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.19-Isa.26.21">Is 26:19-21</reference>).<div eID="gen6900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set time--</hi>a decreed time (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>). <div eID="gen6901" type="x-p"/>
entries.8486d924c06b3bf2520dab4c2ea05e391c4eabc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4748"/><div sID="gen6902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4748"/><hi type="bold">14. shall he live?--</hi>The answer implied is, There is a hope that he shall, though not in the present order of life, as is shown by the words following. Job had denied (<reference osisRef="Job.14.10-Job.14.12">Job 14:10-12</reference>) that man shall live again in this present world. But hoping for a "set time," when God shall remember and raise him out of the hiding-place of the grave (<reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job 14:13</reference>), he declares himself willing to "wait all the days of his appointed time" of continuance in the grave, however long and hard that may be.<div eID="gen6902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appointed time--</hi>literally, "warfare, hard service"; imlying the hardship of being shut out from the realms of life, light, and God for the time he shall be in the grave (<reference osisRef="Job.7.1">Job 7:1</reference>).<div eID="gen6903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">change--</hi>my release, as a soldier at his post released from duty by the relieving guard (see on <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>) [Umbreit and Gesenius], but elsewhere Gesenius explains it, "renovation," as of plants in spring (<reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job 14:7</reference>), but this does not accord so well with the metaphor in "appointed time" or "warfare." <div eID="gen6904" type="x-p"/>
entries.66fa3482ed71702f205610398118e76fe8d30945: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4749"/><div sID="gen6905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4749"/>15. namely, at the resurrection (<reference osisRef="John.5.28">Joh 5:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference>).<div eID="gen6905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have a desire to--</hi>literally, "become pale with anxious desire:" the same word is translated "sore longedst after" (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.30">Ge 31:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">Psa 84:2</reference>), implying the utter unlikelihood that God would leave in oblivion the "creature of His own hands so fearfully and wonderfully made." It is objected that if Job knew of a future retribution, he would make it the leading topic in solving the problem of the permitted afflictions of the righteous. But, (1) He did not intend to exceed the limits of what was clearly revealed; the doctrine was then in a vague form only; (2) The doctrine of God's moral government in this life, even independently of the future, needed vindication. <div eID="gen6906" type="x-p"/>
entries.d501f01b90be9827b337be1e192fd04d53fec86d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4750"/><div sID="gen6907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4750"/>16. Rather, "Yea, thou wilt number my steps, and wilt not (as now) jealously watch over my sin." Thenceforward, instead of severe watching for every sin of Job, God will guard him against every sin.<div eID="gen6907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">number ... steps--</hi>that is, minutely attend to them, that they may not wander [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.9">1Sa 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.23">Psa 37:23</reference>). <div eID="gen6908" type="x-p"/>
entries.692507aa00165aec5b0459b1ad3d39ebc6a1c5bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4751"/><div sID="gen6909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4751"/><hi type="bold">17. sealed up--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.9.7">Job 9:7</reference>). Is shut up in eternal oblivion, that is, God thenceforth will think no more of my former sins. To cover sins is to completely forgive them (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.2">85:2</reference>). Purses of money in the East are usually sealed.<div eID="gen6909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sewest up--</hi>rather, "coverest"; akin to an Arabic word, "to color over," to forget wholly. <div eID="gen6910" type="x-p"/>
entries.76ba814f00bb36542eb07e1153d8540047460116: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4752"/><div sID="gen6911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4752"/><hi type="bold">18. cometh to naught--</hi>literally, "fadeth"; a poetical image from a leaf (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.4">Is 34:4</reference>). Here Job falls back into his gloomy bodings as to the grave. Instead of "and surely," translate "yet"; marking the transition from his brighter hopes. Even the solid mountain falls and crumbles away; man therefore cannot "hope" to escape decay or to live again in the present world (<reference osisRef="Job.14.19">Job 14:19</reference>).<div eID="gen6911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of his place--</hi>so man (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference>). <div eID="gen6912" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa648c67aaa7f3a5bcd6261b61142266b429b892: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4753"/><div sID="gen6913" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4753"/>19. The Hebrew order is more forcible: "Stones themselves are worn away by water."<div eID="gen6913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things which grow out of--</hi>rather, "floods wash away the dust of the earth." There is a gradation from "mountains" to "rocks" (<reference osisRef="Job.14.18">Job 14:18</reference>), then "stones," then last "dust of the earth"; thus the solid mountain at last disappears utterly. <div eID="gen6914" type="x-p"/>
entries.acce0d076b5e0deeddd1c3c14f2843730390ffff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4754"/><div sID="gen6915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4754"/><hi type="bold">20. prevailest--</hi>dost overpower by superior strength.<div eID="gen6915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passeth--</hi>dieth.<div eID="gen6916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">changest countenance--</hi>the change in the visage at death. Differently (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.9">Da 5:9</reference>). <div eID="gen6917" type="x-p"/>
entries.e425af17305418a5e1140553957f911cdbdba2a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4755"/><div sID="gen6918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4755"/>21. One striking trait is selected from the sad picture of the severance of the dead from all that passes in the world (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.5">Ec 9:5</reference>), namely, the utter separation of parents and children. <div eID="gen6918" type="x-p"/>
entries.02f4e6ee2b5678c22641ba635224f22caa6ccc8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4756"/><div sID="gen6919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4756"/>22. "Flesh" and "soul" describe the whole man. Scripture rests the hope of a future life, not on the inherent immortality of the soul, but on the restoration of the body with the soul. In the unseen world, Job in a gloomy frame anticipates, man shall be limited to the thought of his own misery. "Pain is by personification, from our feelings while alive, attributed to the flesh and soul, as if the man could feel in his body when dead. It is the dead in general, not the wicked, who are meant here." <chapter eID="Job.14"/>

entries.0eecaf6745c7cde3fbeb66476f4a127ee691a0e8: <div eID="gen16454" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16455" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16456" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16456" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16455" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16457" type="x-p"/> The shortness, misery, and sinfulness of man's life, <reference osisRef="Job.14.1-Job.14.4">Job 14:1-4</reference>. The unavoidable necessity of death; and the hope of a general resurrection, <reference osisRef="Job.14.5-Job.14.15">Job 14:5-15</reference>. Job deplores his own state, and the general wretchedness of man, <reference osisRef="Job.14.16-Job.14.22">Job 14:16-22</reference>. <div eID="gen16457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16458" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16459" type="x-p"/> Man - born of a woman - There is a delicacy in the original, not often observed: אדם ילוד אשה Adam yelud ishah, "Adam born of a woman, few of days, and full of tremor." Adam, who did not spring from woman, but was immediately formed by God, had many days, for he lived nine hundred and thirty years; during which time neither sin nor death had multiplied in the earth, as they were found in the days of Job. But the Adam who springs now from woman, in the way of ordinary generation, has very few years. Seventy, on an average, being the highest term, may be well said to be few in days; and all matter of fact shows that they are full of fears and apprehensions, רגז rogez, cares, anxieties, and tremors. He seems born, not indeed to live, but to die; and, by living, he forfeits the title to life.
entries.0c646ff385f7fbb8dbd23244d3a5258af3a6a7a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16460" type="x-p"/> He cometh forth like a flower - This is a frequent image both in the Old and New Testament writers; I need not quote the places here, as the readers will find them all in the margin. <div eID="gen16460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16461" type="x-p"/> He fleeth also as a shadow - Himself, as he appears among men, is only the shadow of his real, substantial, and eternal being. He is here compared to a vegetable; he springs up, bears his flower is often nipped by disease, blasted by afflictions and at last cut down by death. The bloom of youth, even in the most prosperous state, is only the forerunner of hoary hairs, enfeebled muscles, impaired senses, general debility, anility, and dissolution. All these images are finely embodied, and happily expressed, in the beautiful lines of a very nervous and correct poet, too little known, but whose compositions deserve the first place among what may be called the minor poets of Britain. See at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.14.22">Job 14:22</reference> (note).
entries.b0253da7879847c12e1a9f93420e17ba59206f09: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16462" type="x-p"/> Dost thou open thine eyes upon such a one - The whole of this chapter is directed to God alone; in no part of it does he take any notice of his friends.
entries.80e8c51127bb5b7f40f292e4c43a8613114126aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16463" type="x-p"/> Who can bring a clean thing - This verse is thus rendered by the Chaldee: "Who will produce a clean thing from man, who is polluted with sins, except God, who is one?" By Coverdale thus: Who can make it cleane, that commeth of an uncleane thinge? No body. The text refers to man's original and corrupt nature. Every man that is born into the world comes into it in a corrupt or sinful state. This is called original sin; and is derived from fallen Adam, who is the stock, to the utmost ramifications of the human family. Not one human spirit is born into the world without this corruption of nature. All are impure and unholy; and from this principle of depravity all transgression is produced; and from this corruption of nature God alone can save. The Septuagint, in the Codex Alexandrinus, reads the verse thus: Τις γαρ εσται καθαρο· απο ῥυπου; ουδε εἱς, εαν και μιας ἡμερας γενηται ὁ βιος αυτου επι της γης; "Who is pure from corruption? Not one, although he had lived but one day upon the earth."
entries.2fbc85ab476702bb746accb1b819a0cba7520e5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16464" type="x-p"/> Seeing his days are determined - The general term of human life is fixed by God himself; in vain are all attempts to prolong it beyond this term. Several attempts have been made in all nations to find an elixir that would expel all the seeds of disease, and keep men in continual health; but all these attempts have failed. Basil, Valentine, Norton, Dastin, Ripley, Sandivogius, Artephius, Geber, Van Helmont, Paracelsus, Philalethes, and several others, both in Europe and Asia, have written copiously on the subject, and have endeavored to prove that a tincture might be produced, by which all imperfect metals may be transmuted into perfect; and an elixir by which the human body may be kept in a state of endless repair and health. And these profess to teach the method by which this tincture and this elixir may be made! Yet all these are dead; and dead, for aught we know, comparatively young! Artephius is, indeed, said to have lived ninety years, which is probable; but some of his foolish disciples, to give credit to their thriftless craft, added another cipher, and made his age nine hundred! Man may endeavor to pass the bound; and God may, here and there, produce a Thomas Parr, who died in 1635, aged one hundred and fifty-two; and a Henry Jenkins, who died in 1670, aged one hundred and sixty-nine; but these are rare instances, and do not affect the general term. Nor can death be avoided. Dust thou art, and unto dust thou shalt return, is the law, and that will ever render nugatory all such pretended tinctures and elixirs. But, although man cannot pass his appointed bounds, yet he may so live as never to reach them; for folly and wickedness abridge the term of human life; and therefore the psalmist says, Bloody and deceitful men shall not live out Half their days, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.23">Psa 55:23</reference>, for by indolence, intemperance, and disorderly passions, the life of man is shortened in cases innumerable. We are not to understand the bounds as applying to individuals, but to the race in general. Perhaps there is no case in which God has determined absolutely that man's age shall be so long, and shall neither be more nor less. The contrary supposition involves innumerable absurdities.
entries.4c24c4b40f70f70754e4a1da2f98427c75fec608: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16465" type="x-p"/> Turn from him, that he may rest - Cease to try him by afflictions and distresses, that he may enjoy some of the comforts of life, before he be removed from it: and thus, like a hireling, who is permitted by his master to take a little repose in the heat of the day, from severe labor, I shall also have a breathing time from affliction, before I come to that bound over which I cannot pass. See <reference osisRef="Job.10.20">Job 10:20</reference> (note), where there is a similar request.
entries.e8d93c45a384a657cfd69317733d6811b20ec9b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16466" type="x-p"/> For there is hope of a tree - We must not, says Calmet, understand this of an old tree, the stem and roots of which are dried up and rotted: but there are some trees which grow from cuttings, and some which, though pulled out of the earth, and having had their roots dried and withered by long exposure to the sun and wind, will, on being replanted, take root and resume their verdure. There are also certain trees, the fibres of which are so solid, that if after several years they be steeped in water, they resume their vigor, the tubes dilate, and the blossoms or flowers which were attached to them expand; as I have often witnessed in what is called the rose of Jericho. There are few trees which will not send forth new shoots, when the stock is cut down level with the earth.
entries.651af89863ed3a28cf065b4e8344f31f91037759: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16467" type="x-p"/> Through the scent of water it will bud - A fine metaphor: the water acts upon the decaying and perishing tree, as strong and powerful odors from musk, otto of roses, ammonia, etc., act on a fainting or swooning person.
entries.c66f9ed6bd2e196cb5de7e4289f1d455530bdccf: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16468" type="x-p"/> But man dieth - No human being ever can spring from the dead body of man; that wasteth away, corrupts, and is dissolved; for the man dies; and when he breathes out his last breath, and his body is reduced to dust, then, where is he? There is a beautiful verse in the Persian poet Khosroo, that is not unlike this saying of Job: - "I went towards the burying ground, and wept <div eID="gen16468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16469" type="x-p"/> To think of the departure of friends which were captives to death; <div eID="gen16469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16470" type="x-p"/> I said, Where are they! and Fate <div eID="gen16470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16471" type="x-p"/> Gave back this answer by Echo, Where are they? <div eID="gen16471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16472" type="x-p"/> Thus paraphrased by a learned friend: - <div eID="gen16472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16473" type="x-p"/> Beneath the cypress' solemn shade, <div eID="gen16473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16474" type="x-p"/> As on surrounding tombs I gazed, <div eID="gen16474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16475" type="x-p"/> I wept, and thought of friends there laid, <div eID="gen16475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16476" type="x-p"/> Whose hearts with warmest love had blazed. <div eID="gen16476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16477" type="x-p"/> Where are those friends my heart doth lack, <div eID="gen16477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16478" type="x-p"/> Whose words, in grief, gave peace? Ah, where? <div eID="gen16478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16479" type="x-p"/> And Fate, by Echo, gave me back <div eID="gen16479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16480" type="x-p"/> This short but just reply, Ah, where?
entries.7628eb808b35fb3d3f2840e63ebc475380edf8e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16481" type="x-p"/> The waters fail from the sea - I believe this refers to evaporation, and nothing else. As the waters are evaporated from the sea, and the river in passing over the sandy desert is partly exsiccated, and partly absorbed; and yet the waters of the sea are not exhausted, as these vapors, being condensed, fall down in rain, and by means of rivers return again into the sea: so man is imperceptibly removed from his fellows by death and dissolution; yet the human race is still continued, the population of the earth being kept up by perpetual generations.
entries.a55ca601b58b72acd13f13935877710c57a6566d: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16482" type="x-p"/> So man lieth down - He falls asleep in his bed of earth. <div eID="gen16482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16483" type="x-p"/> And riseth not - Men shall not, like cut down trees and plants, reproduce their like; nor shall they arise till the heavens are no more, till the earth and all its works are burnt up, and the general resurrection of human beings shall take place. Surely it would be difficult to twist this passage to the denial of the resurrection of the body. Neither can these expressions be fairly understood as implying Job's belief in the materiality of the soul, and that the whole man sleeps from the day of his death to the morning of the resurrection. We have already seen that Job makes a distinction between the animal life and rational soul in man; and it is most certain that the doctrine of the materiality of the soul, and its sleep till the resurrection, has no place in the sacred records. There is a most beautiful passage to the same purpose, and with the same imagery, in Moschus's epitaph on the death of Bion: - Αι, αι ται μαλαχαι μεν επαν κατα καπον ολωνται, Η τα χλωρα σελινα, το τ' ευθαλες ουλον ανηθον, Ὑστερον αυ ζωοντι, και εις ετος αλλο φυοντι· Αμμες δ', οἱ μεγαλοι, και καρτεροι, η σοφοι ανδρες, Ὁπποτε πρωτα θανωμες, ανακοοι εν χθονι κοιλα Εὑδομες ευ μαλα μακρον, ατερμονα, νηγρετον ὑπνον. <div eID="gen16483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16484" type="x-p"/> Idyll. iii., ver. 100. <div eID="gen16484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16485" type="x-p"/> Alas! alas! the mallows, when they die, <div eID="gen16485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16486" type="x-p"/> Or garden herbs, and sweet Anethum's pride, <div eID="gen16486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16487" type="x-p"/> Blooming in vigor, wake again to life, <div eID="gen16487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16488" type="x-p"/> And flourish beauteous through another year: <div eID="gen16488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16489" type="x-p"/> But we, the great, the mighty, and the wise, <div eID="gen16489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16490" type="x-p"/> When once we die, unknown in earth's dark womb <div eID="gen16490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16491" type="x-p"/> Sleep long and drear, the endless sleep of death. <div eID="gen16491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16492" type="x-p"/> J. B. B. C. <div eID="gen16492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16493" type="x-p"/> A more cold and comfortless philosophy was never invented. The next verse shows that Job did not entertain this view of the subject.
entries.30055fc753b8e637233847bececfa6f683022695: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16494" type="x-p"/> O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave - Dreadful as death is to others, I shall esteem it a high privilege; it will be to me a covert from the wind and from the tempest of this affliction and distress. <div eID="gen16494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16495" type="x-p"/> Keep me secret - Hide my soul with thyself, where my enemies cannot invade my repose; or, as the poet expresses it: - "My spirit hide with saints above, <div eID="gen16495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16496" type="x-p"/> My body in the tomb." <div eID="gen16496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16497" type="x-p"/> Job does not appear to have the same thing in view when he entreats God to hide him in the grave; and to keep him secret, until his wrath be past. The former relates to the body; the latter to the spirit. <div eID="gen16497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16498" type="x-p"/> That thou wouldest appoint me a set time - As he had spoken of the death of his body before, and the secreting of his spirit in the invisible world, he must refer here to the resurrection; for what else can be said to be an object of desire to one whose body is mingled with the dust? <div eID="gen16498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16499" type="x-p"/> And remember me! - When my body has paid that debt of death which it owes to thy Divine justice, and the morning of the resurrection is come, when it may be said thy wrath, אפך appecha, "thy displeasure," against the body is past, it having suffered the sentence denounced by thyself: Dust thou art, and unto dust thou shalt return, for in the day thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die; then remember me - raise my body, unite my spirit to it, and receive both into thy glory for ever.
entries.2f7e398c13c4ca37b5580a0c109119af9443f233: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16500" type="x-p"/> If a man die, shall he live again? - The Chaldee translates, If a wicked man die, can he ever live again? or, he can never live again. The Syriac and Arabic thus: "If a man die, shall he revive? Yea, all the days of his youth he awaits till his old age come." The Septuagint: "If a man die, shall he live, having accomplished the days of his life? I will endure till I live again." Here is no doubt, but a strong persuasion, of the certainty of the general resurrection. <div eID="gen16500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16501" type="x-p"/> All the days of my appointed time - צבאי tsebai, "of my warfare;" see on <reference osisRef="Job.7.1">Job 7:1</reference> (note). Will I await till חליפתי chaliphathi, my renovation, come. This word is used to denote the springing again of grass, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.5">Psa 90:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.90.6">Psa 90:6</reference>, after it had once withered, which is in itself a very expressive emblem of the resurrection.
entries.467da0b73694e40e1c31c18df15cff7aaf05c13f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16502" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt call - Thou shalt say There shall be time no longer: Awake, ye dead! and come to judgment! <div eID="gen16502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16503" type="x-p"/> And I will answer thee - My dissolved frame shall be united at thy call; and body and soul shall be rejoined. <div eID="gen16503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16504" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt have a desire - תכסף tichsoph, "Thou wilt pant with desire;" or, "Thou wilt yearn over the work of thy hands." God has subjected the creature to vanity, in hope; having determined the resurrection. Man is one of the noblest works of God. He has exhibited him as a master-piece of his creative skill, power, and goodness. Nothing less than the strongest call upon justice could have induced him thus to destroy the work of his hands. No wonder that he has an earnest desire towards it; and that although man dies, and is as water spilt upon the ground that cannot be gathered up again; yet doth he devise means that his banished be not expelled from him. Even God is represented as earnestly longing for the ultimate reviviscence of the sleeping dust. He cannot, he will not, forget the work of his hands.
entries.622dcdaee1bcc9c9e8ae1111a985282b393cab02: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16505" type="x-p"/> For now thou numberest my steps - כי עתה ki attah, Although thou, etc. Though thou, by thy conduct towards me, seemest bent on my utter destruction, yet thou delightest in mercy, and I shall be saved.
entries.bdc64fe138c372a59b6c8aca520a65c088fae981: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16506" type="x-p"/> My transgression is sealed up in a bag - An allusion to the custom of collecting evidence of state transgressions, sealing them up in a bag, and presenting them to the judges and officers of state to be examined, in order to trial and judgment. Just at this time (July, 1820) charges of state transgressions, sealed up in a Green Bag, and presented to the two houses of parliament, for the examination of a secret committee, are making a considerable noise in the land. Some suppose the allusion is to money sealed up in bags; which is common in the East. This includes two ideas: <div eID="gen16506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16507" type="x-p"/> 1. Job's transgressions were all numbered; not one was passed by. <div eID="gen16507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16508" type="x-p"/> 2. They were sealed up; so that none of them could be lost. These bags were indifferently sewed or sealed, the two words in the text.
entries.3455b21926eefaaeadcb431ff6e27a02ff4cbe83: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16509" type="x-p"/> The mountain falling cometh to naught - Every thing in nature is exposed to mutability and decay: - even mountains themselves may fall from their bases, and be dashed to pieces; or be suddenly swallowed up by an earthquake; and, by the same means, the strongest and most massive rocks may be removed.
entries.b670dfc768be7cd71ad44f7e8b232ee604718f0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16510" type="x-p"/> The waters wear the stones - Even the common stones are affected in the same way. Were even earthquakes and violent concussions of nature wanting, the action of water, either running over them as a stream, or even falling upon them in drops, will wear these stones. Hence the proverb: - <div eID="gen16510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16511" type="x-p"/> Gutta cavat lapidem non vi sed saepe cadendo. "Constant droppings will make a hole in a flint." Εκ θαμινης ραθαμιγγος, ὁκως λογος, αιες ιοισας, Χ' ἁ λιθος ες ρωχμον κοιλαινεται. "From frequent dropping, as the proverb says, perpetually falling, even a stone is hollowed into a hole." <div eID="gen16511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16512" type="x-p"/> Thou washest away the things - Alluding to sudden falls of rain occasioning floods, by which the fruits of the earth are swept away; and thus the hope of man - the grain for his household, and provender for his cattle, is destroyed.
entries.7a911d5cb4fd1a67b7fdd9d9aa8a41cdfc7b27c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16513" type="x-p"/> Thou prevailest for ever against him - It is impossible for him to withstand thee: every stroke of thine brings him down. <div eID="gen16513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16514" type="x-p"/> Thou changest his countenance - Probably an allusion to the custom of covering the face, when the person was condemned, and sending him away to execution. See the case of Haman, in the note on Esther, <reference osisRef="Est.7.8">Est 7:8</reference> (note).
entries.84e017f652d42168b7567c8aedf62957f0b1975e: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16515" type="x-p"/> His sons come to honor - When dead, he is equally indifferent and unconscious whether his children have met with a splendid or oppressive lot in life; for as to this world, when man dies, in that day all his thoughts perish.
entries.f9da5378524b1d5de84f9c3751468159cd5aace3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16516" type="x-p"/> But his flesh upon him shall have pain - The sum of the life of man is this, pain of body and distress of soul; and he is seldom without the one or the other, and often oppressed by both. Thus ends Job's discourse on the miserable state and condition of man. The last verse of the preceding chapter has been differently translated and explained. Mr. <div eID="gen16516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16517" type="x-p"/> Good's version is the following, which he vindicates in a learned note: - <div eID="gen16517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16518" type="x-p"/> For his flesh shall drop away from him; <div eID="gen16518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16519" type="x-p"/> And his soul shall become a waste from him. <div eID="gen16519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16520" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee thus: "Nevertheless his flesh, on account of the worms, shall grieve over him; and his soul, in the house of judgment, shall wail over him." In another copy of this version it is thus: "Nevertheless his flesh, before the window is closed over him, shall grieve; and his soul, for seven days of mourning, shall bewail him in the house of his burial." I shall give the Hebrew: - אך בשרו עליו יכאב <div eID="gen16520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16521" type="x-p"/> Ach besaro alaiv yichab, ונפשו עליו תאבל <div eID="gen16521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16522" type="x-p"/> Venaphsho alaiv teebal. <div eID="gen16522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16523" type="x-p"/> Which Mr. Stock translates thus, both to the spirit and letter: - <div eID="gen16523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16524" type="x-p"/> But over him his flesh shall grieve; <div eID="gen16524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16525" type="x-p"/> And over him his breath shall mourn. "In the daring spirit of oriental poetry," says he, "the flesh, or body, and the breath, are made conscious beings; the former lamenting its putrefaction in the grave, the latter mourning over the mouldering clay which it once enlivened." <div eID="gen16525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16526" type="x-p"/> This version is, in my opinion, the most natural yet offered. The Syriac and Arabic present nearly the same sense: "But his body shall grieve over him; and his soul be astonished over him." <div eID="gen16526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16527" type="x-p"/> Coverdale follows the Vulgate: Whyle he lyveth his flesh must have travayle; and whyle the soul is in him, he must be in sorowe. <div eID="gen16527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16528" type="x-p"/> On <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job 14:2</reference>. I have referred to the following beautiful lines, which illustrate these finely figurative texts: - <div eID="gen16528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16529" type="x-p"/> He cometh forth as a Flower, and is Cut Down; he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not. <div eID="gen16529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16530" type="x-p"/> All flesh is Grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the Flower of the field. <div eID="gen16530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16531" type="x-p"/> The Grass withereth, the Flower fadeth; but the word of our God shall stand for ever. <div eID="gen16531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16532" type="x-p"/> The morning flowers display their sweets,And gay their silken leaves unfold; <div eID="gen16532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16533" type="x-p"/> As careless of the noonday heats,As fearless of the evening cold. <div eID="gen16533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16534" type="x-p"/> Nipp'd by the wind's untimely blast,Parch'd by the sun's directer ray, <div eID="gen16534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16535" type="x-p"/> The momentary glories waste,The short-lived beauties die away. <div eID="gen16535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16536" type="x-p"/> So blooms the human face divine,When youth its pride of beauty shows;
