By way of opposition, <ns0:hi>The Waters go, or flow out of the Sea,</ns0:hi> and return thither again, <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 1. 7. <ns0:hi>and a Lake,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>River</ns0:hi> sometimes <ns0:hi>decayeth, and drieth up;</ns0:hi> but af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terwards is recruited and replenished. <ns0:hi>But man lieth,</ns0:hi> &c. as it fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lows. Or 2. By way of resemblance. As <ns0:hi>Waters, i. e.</ns0:hi> some porti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of Waters, <ns0:hi>fail from the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>a,</ns0:hi> being either exhaled or drawn up by the Sun, or received and sunk into the dry and thirsty Earth, or overflowing its Banks; <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>the Flood</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a River,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a Pond,</ns0:hi> (for the word signifies any considerable confluence of Waters) in a great drought <ns0:hi>decayeth, and is dried up:</ns0:hi> in both which cases the self same Waters never return to their former places. So it is with man. Or thus, as <ns0:hi>when the Waters fail from the Sea, i. e.</ns0:hi> when the Sea forsakes the place into which it used to flow, <ns0:hi>the River</ns0:hi> which was fed by it, <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 1. 7. <ns0:hi>decayeth and drieth up</ns0:hi> without all hopes of Recovery. So man, when once the Fountain of his radical moi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sture is dried up, dies, and never revives again.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. So man lieth down <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To wit, in his Bed, the Grave, or to sleep the sleep of Death<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> as this Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 46. 30. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 31. 16. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 12. 1 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 1. 21.</ns0:note>, and riseth not <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To wit, to this Life: For he speaks not here of the Life to come, nor of the Resurrection of the Body after death by the divine Power; of his belief whereof he giveth sufficient evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dences in divers places.</ns0:note>, till the Heavens <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> no more <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Either 1. Never; because the Heavens, though they shall be changed in their Qualities, yet shall never cease to be as to the Substance of them. And therefore everlasting and unchangeable things are expressed by the duration of the Heavens; of which see <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 72. 5, 7, 17. & 89. 30, 36, 37. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 5. 18. & 24. 35. Or 2. not until the time of the general Resurrection, and the restitution of things, when these visible Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vens shall pass away, and be no more, at least in the same form and manner as now they are: of which see <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 102. 26. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 21. 33. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3. 7, 10. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 21. 1.</ns0:note>, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their Sleep.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. O that thou wouldest hide me in <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> the Grave <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. In some dark Vault under ground, such as good men hide themselves in, in times of Persecution. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11. 38. Lord hide me in some hiding place from thy Wrath, and all the intolerable effects of it, which are upon me: for I cannot be hid from thee but by thee. Or 2. In the Grave, properly so called. Though I know Life once lost is irrecoverable, yet I heartily de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sire Death rather than to continue in these Torments. And if the next words and wish seem to suppose the continuance of his Life, that is not strange: For he speaks like one almost distracted with his miseries, sometimes wishing one thing, sometimes another, and the quite contrary, as such persons use to do. And these Wishes may be understood disjunctively, I wish either that I were dead, or that God would give me Life free from these torments. Or the place may be understood thus, I could wish, if it were possible, that I might lie in the Grave for a time, till these storms be blown over, and then be restored to a comfortable Life.</ns0:note>, that thou wouldst keep me secret <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">In some se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cret and safe place, under the shadow of thy Wings and favour. that I may have some support and comfort from thee.</ns0:note>, until thy Wrath be past <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Whilst I am oppressed with such grievous and various Calamities, which he calls Gods <ns0:hi>Wrath,</ns0:hi> because they were, or seemed to be, the ef<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fects of his Wrath.</ns0:note>, that thou wouldst appoint me a set time <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit, to my sufferings, as thou hast done to my Life, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5.</ns0:note>, and remember me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Wherein thou wiltst remember me, to wit, in mercy, o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> so as to deliver me: For it is well known that God is frequently said to <ns0:hi>forget</ns0:hi> those whom he suffers to continue in misery, and to <ns0:hi>remember</ns0:hi> those whom he delivers out of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. If a man die, shall he live <ns0:hi>again</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He shall not<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> namely in this World, as was said before. The affirmative question is equivalent to an absolute denial, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 18. 17. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 56. 7. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 5. 9. and every where.</ns0:note>? all the days of <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> my warfare.</ns0:note> my appointed time will I wait till my change come <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Seeing Death puts an end to all mens hopes of any comfortable being here, because man once dead never returns to Life; I will therefore wait on God, and hope for his favour whilest I live, and it is possible to enjoy it, and will continue waiting from time to time, <ns0:hi>until my change come, i. e.</ns0:hi> either 1. Death, the great and last change; which is expressed by the Root of this word, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 10. 17. Or 2. The change of my condition for the better, which you upon your Terms en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />courage me to expect, and which I yet trust in God I shall enjoy; for this word properly signifies <ns0:hi>Vicissitudes</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Changes</ns0:hi> in ones condi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and this seems to suit best with the following verse. And this Change, or a comfortable Life here <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> so heartily wisheth, not only from that love of Life and Comfort which is naturally im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />planted in all men, good and bad, and is not forbidden by God, which also was stronger in those Old Testament Saints when the discoveries of Gods Grace to sinners, and of eternal Life, were much darker than now they are; but also because this would be an effectual vindication of his own Integrity, and Good-name, and of the honour of Religion, both which did suffer some Eclipse from <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s extream Calamities, as is evident from the discourses of his Friends.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. Thou shalt <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 40. 3.</ns0:note> call, and I will answer thee <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">I trust there is a time coming when thou wiltst grant me the mercy which now thou deniest me, to wit, a favourable hearing, when thou <ns0:hi>wiltst call</ns0:hi> to me to speak for my self, and <ns0:hi>I shall answer thee;</ns0:hi> which I know will be to thy Satisfaction and my Comfort. Compare this with <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 13. 22. where the same words are used in this same Sense. Or, <ns0:hi>thou shalt call</ns0:hi> me out of the Grave of my Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lamities, <ns0:hi>and I shall answer thee,</ns0:hi> and say, Here I am, raised out of the Pit in which I was buried by thy powerful and gracious Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand.</ns0:note>: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To me who am thy Workmanship in divers respects, from whom thou now seemest to have an aversion and abhorrency, but I doubt not thou wiltst have a <ns0:hi>desire, i. e.</ns0:hi> shew thy Affection or Good-will to me; or a desire to look upon me, and to deliver me. Nor is it strange that <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> who lately was upon the brink of despair, doth now breath out words of Hope, such Ebbings and Flowings be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing usual, both with <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> elsewhere, as <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 13. 15, 16. and with <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> frequently in the Psalms, and with others of God's Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 139. 2, 3. Chap. 13. 27. Prov. 5. 21. Jer. 32. 19.</ns0:note> For now <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">So this is a reason of his desire of Death, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 13. Or rather, <ns0:hi>But now;</ns0:hi> for this seems to be added by way of opposition. I believe thou wiltst pitty and help me, but for the present it is far otherwise with me.</ns0:note> thou numbrest my steps <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Thou makest a strict enquiry into all my Actions, that thou maist find out all mine Errours, and punish them. Compare <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 13. 27. & 31. 4. & 34. 21. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 56. 6.</ns0:note>, dost thou not watch over my sin <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Dost thou not watch for my Haltings, or Miscarriages, as if thou wast glad of an occasion to punish me? Or, <ns0:hi>thou dost not delay the punishment of my sin:</ns0:hi> For the same Hebrew word signifies both <ns0:hi>sin,</ns0:hi> and its <ns0:hi>punish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. My transgression <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> sealed up in a bag <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">As Writings or other choice things, that they may be safely kept, and all of them brought forth upon occasion, and not one of them forgotten or lost. Compare <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 34. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 37. 7. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 13. 12.</ns0:note>, and thou sewest up mine iniquity <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou keepest all my sins in thy memory, and fastenest the guilt of them upon my Conscience. Or, <ns0:hi>thou addest to my sin,</ns0:hi> one sin to another, the follies of my youth, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 13. 26. to those of my riper Years. Or, <ns0:hi>thou addest to my punishment, i. e.</ns0:hi> thou punishest me more than mine Iniquities deserve, all things considered. For this sinful thought seems somtimes to have risen in <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s Mind, as may be gathered from divers parts of this Book: which therefore <ns0:hi>Zophar</ns0:hi> decries, and disproves, <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 11. 6.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. And surely as the Mountain falling <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> sad<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> cometh to nought <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">As when a great <ns0:hi>Mountain falls,</ns0:hi> either by an Earthquake or Inundation of Waters, or from any other cause, it <ns0:hi>moulders away like a fading Leaf,</ns0:hi> (as the Hebrew word signifies) and never recovers its former height and stability, <ns0:hi>and as the Rock</ns0:hi> when by the vio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lence of Winds or Earthquake, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> it <ns0:hi>is removed out of its place,</ns0:hi> and thrown down is never readvanced. And as <ns0:hi>the waters</ns0:hi> by continual droppings, or violent and frequent assaults, <ns0:hi>wear away,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>break the stones to pieces,</ns0:hi> so as they can never be made whole again: And as <ns0:hi>thou washest away,</ns0:hi> to wit, by a great and violent Inundation which thou sendest, <ns0:hi>the things which grow out of the dust of the Earth,</ns0:hi> to wit, Herbs, & Fruits, & Plants, which once washed away are irrecoverably lost, <ns0:hi>and,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> (as this particle is oft used, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> in like manner, to wit, irrecoverably,) <ns0:hi>thou destroyest the hope of man; i. e.</ns0:hi> So when man dies all hope of living again in this World is utterly lost, And this seems to be the plain meaning of these two Verses. And as be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore he declared the hopelesness of mans restauration from death to this animal life, by way of opposition to such things as did rise in a manner from death to life, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> so now he declares it by way of similitude or resemblance to such things as being once lost and gone, are past all hopes of recovery.</ns0:note>: and the Rock is removed out of his place:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:396" />19. The Waters wear the Stones: thou <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />flowest.</ns0:note> washest away the things which grow <ns0:hi>out</ns0:hi> of the Dust of the Earth, and thou destroyest the hope of Man.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. Thou prevailest for ever against him <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">When once thou takest away this life it is gone for ever: For he speaks not here of man's future and eternal life in another World.</ns0:note>, and he passeth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He dieth or is about to die: Man's death is oft called a <ns0:hi>passage</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a going;</ns0:hi> to intimate that it is not an annihila<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, but only a translation of him into another place and state.</ns0:note>: thou changest his Countenance <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either 1 his Visage, which by death and its Harbingers, is quite transformed in colour and shape, as we see by daily experience. Or 2. the face and state of his Affairs, as to worldly riches and pleasures, and honours, all which he leaves behind him.</ns0:note>, and send<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est him away <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To his long home by death.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either 1. is ignorant of all such events: Or, 2. is not con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerned nor affected with them. A dead or dying man minds not these things.</ns0:note>; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> not of them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This is mans condition, he is miserable <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>oth when he dies, because he dies without hope of returning to life, as he had dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />coursed before; and (as he now adds) whilest he lives, whilest <ns0:hi>his flesh</ns0:hi> is <ns0:hi>upon him, and his soul within him;</ns0:hi> whilest the soul is clothed with or united to the body, he feels sharp <ns0:hi>pain</ns0:hi> in his bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy, and bitter grief in his soul, Seeing therefore the state of man upon earth is so vain and unhappy every way, Lord give me some comfort to sweeten my life, or take away my life from me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
